lines: Lecture 4. Hellenistic and Roman Philosophy. Medieval Philosophy
Stoicism, Epicureanism, skepticism, Neoplatonism; patristics (Augustine); scholasticism (Thomas Aquinas); the dispute over universals.
[00:00–01:27] INTRODUCTION

In 323 BCE Alexander the Great dies, and with his death it is not only an empire that collapses but the entire familiar horizon of Greek life. The polis, the self-sufficient city-state for whose sake Socrates accepted death and for which Plato and Aristotle built their political utopias, ceases to be the center of the universe for the individual human being: now he lives in vast, impersonal Hellenistic monarchies, where decisions are made far away from him and almost nothing depends on his will. Philosophy, which only yesterday was occupied with grand questions about the structure of the cosmos and the nature of the ideal state, is forced to answer a much more urgent and personal question: how can an individual preserve inner calm and dignity in a world he no longer controls?

Today we will travel a long road — from the Hellenistic schools of practical wisdom, Stoicism, Epicureanism, and Skepticism, through the mystical synthesis of Neoplatonism, to the moment when Greek philosophy meets Christianity and is forced to rethink all its concepts in the light of the idea of a personal, almighty God. We will see Augustine, for whom philosophy becomes a confession, and Thomas Aquinas, who eight centuries later will try to reconcile faith and reason by means of Aristotelian logic, and we will conclude with one of the longest and most productive philosophical disputes in history — the dispute over universals, which for many centuries will determine how European thought understands the relation between general concepts and particular things.
[01:27–04:08] SECTION 1. STOICISM: FREEDOM THROUGH AGREEMENT WITH NATURE

The Stoic school was founded in Athens around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium, and the school took its name from the Painted Stoa, the portico where he held his conversations. The basis of Stoic physics is the idea of the cosmos as a single, rationally ordered, ensouled whole, permeated by logos — a concept that, as you remember from the first lecture, goes back to Heraclitus. Everything that happens in the world is subject to a strict chain of causes, to fate, to destiny, and no single event can happen otherwise than it does.

From this physics, the Stoics derive the ethics that became the school's most influential legacy. If everything in the world is predetermined by rational providence, then the only thing that is truly within our power is not external circumstances, but our own judgment about them, our agreement or disagreement with what is happening. The famous Stoic distinction between what depends on us and what does not depend on us, worked out in detail by the later Stoic Epictetus, leads to a practical conclusion: the sage must direct all his energy toward governing his own judgments, desires, and impulses, giving up entirely any anxiety about health, wealth, reputation, or even one's own life — things which the Stoic philosophers called "indifferents," since they do not depend on our will. The highest state of the Stoic sage is apatheia, literally "passionlessness," freedom from destructive affects, fear, anger, envy, achieved not by suppressing feelings, but by a correct, rational judgment about what is truly valuable and what is not. The Stoic ideal is beautifully summed up by the later Roman Stoic, Emperor Marcus Aurelius, who wrote for himself: it is not things that trouble people, but their opinions about things — a phrase that two thousand years later would become, almost word for word, the foundation of cognitive psychotherapy.

Stoic logic, developed above all by Chrysippus, the third scholarch (head) of the school, supplemented Aristotelian syllogistic with a theory of propositions and conditional inferences, laying the foundations of what in the twentieth century would be called propositional logic, as distinct from Aristotelian term logic. No less important for our course is the Stoic doctrine of the cosmopolis, the world city: since logos, the rational principle, permeates the entire cosmos and is present in every human being regardless of origin, citizenship, or social status, all people, according to the Stoics, are citizens of a single world state, bound by the bonds of rational nature before the bonds of the polis or the tribe. This idea of universal human brotherhood, radically new for Greek thought, which was tied to the polis, will have a profound influence on Roman law and, through it, on later concepts of natural law and human rights, to which we will return in the part of the course devoted to social and political philosophy.
[04:08–06:54] SECTION 2. EPICUREANISM: PLEASURE AS THE ABSENCE OF ANXIETY

Epicurus, who founded his school in Athens around the same time as Zeno, proposed a competing system which the later tradition distorted so much that the word "Epicurean" became a synonym for a hedonist obsessed with luxury and sensual pleasures — the exact opposite of the original teaching. Epicurus did indeed proclaim pleasure as the highest good, but by this he meant above all the absence of bodily suffering and, more importantly, the absence of mental anxiety, ataraxia, rather than the accumulation of intense pleasures. He distinguished between natural and necessary pleasures, natural but unnecessary pleasures, and unnatural and unnecessary pleasures, and insisted that a truly wise life is built on the satisfaction of the simplest, natural, and necessary needs — modest food, a roof over one's head, friendship — since it is precisely the pursuit of excessive, unnatural desires that produces the greater part of human suffering.

Epicurus's physics was based on Democritus's atomism, which we discussed in the previous lecture, but it introduced a fundamental innovation: the concept of the clinamen, a random swerve of an atom from its straight downward path, predetermined by nothing. Democritus's world was rigidly determined by necessity, and Epicurus saw in this a threat to human freedom — if even our thoughts and decisions are completely predetermined by the mechanical movement of atoms, then there can be no question of moral responsibility. By introducing an element of chance into the very physical basis of the world, Epicurus created space for free will within a materialist picture of reality. The practical aim of Epicurean philosophy is to free a person from the two main sources of anxiety: fear of the gods and fear of death. The gods, he argued, do indeed exist, but they remain in a state of perfect blessedness and do not interfere in human affairs in any way, so fearing their anger is pointless; and death, according to the famous Epicurean aphorism, has nothing to do with us at all, since while we exist, death is not yet here, and when death comes, we are no longer here — and therefore it cannot be an object of rational fear.

Three centuries later the Roman poet and philosopher Lucretius would set out Epicurus's entire system in his grand didactic poem On the Nature of Things, which became the main channel through which atomistic physics reached the philosophers of the early modern period. Epicurus also developed one of the first social-contract theories of justice in the history of philosophy: justice, he argued, does not exist in itself, like a Platonic idea, but arises from the mutual agreement of people neither to inflict harm on one another nor to suffer harm from one another — a convention useful for living together safely, not a reflection of an eternal cosmic order. This seemingly modest idea stands at the origins of the entire later contractualist tradition in political philosophy, to which we will return when discussing Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau in the relevant lectures of the course.
[06:54–09:41] SECTION 3. SKEPTICISM: WISDOM AS WITHHOLDING JUDGMENT

The third great Hellenistic school, skepticism, goes back to Pyrrho of Elis and receives systematic development in the works of Sextus Empiricus at the end of antiquity. If the Stoics and Epicureans offered positive teachings about the nature of the world and the highest good, the skeptics called into question the very possibility of attaining reliable knowledge about anything at all. Their main argument was built around the equal force of opposing judgments, isostheneia: on any question about the nature of things, one can find equally convincing arguments for and against, and reason has no reliable criterion by which to give preference to one side of the dispute.

The practical conclusion of the skeptics is paradoxical and in this sense echoes the Jain anekantavada that we discussed in the second lecture: since reliable knowledge is unattainable, the sage must suspend final judgment, epoché, about the nature of things — and it is precisely this withholding, and not the attainment of positive knowledge, that brings peace of mind, ataraxia. The skeptic does not deny the existence of the world and does not affirm its absence — he simply refuses to render a categorical judgment one way or the other, while continuing to act in everyday life in accordance with appearances and accepted customs, without granting them the status of ultimate truth.

It is worth distinguishing two historical currents of skepticism: Pyrrhonism, going directly back to Pyrrho and systematized by Sextus Empiricus, demanded complete, universal withholding of judgment on every question without exception, including the very thesis about the impossibility of knowledge — otherwise skepticism would contradict itself. Academic skepticism, developed by Arcesilaus and Carneades within the walls of Plato's Academy, took a more moderate position: complete certainty is indeed unattainable, but some judgments are more plausible than others, and the sage may well be guided in practical life by the degree of this plausibility, while not claiming absolute truth. Carneades became famous when, having come to Rome as an envoy in 155 BCE, he delivered one day a brilliant speech in defense of justice and the next day an equally brilliant speech proving that it is conventional and relative, to the horror of the conservative Roman senator Cato the Elder, who saw in this a danger to public morality — an episode that perfectly illustrates the virtuosity of skeptical rhetoric inherited from Gorgias, which we discussed in the previous lecture.

Notice the overall logic of all three Hellenistic schools, despite all the differences in their metaphysical premises: the Stoics find peace in agreement with the rational order of the world, the Epicureans — in the satisfaction of the simplest needs and freedom from fear, the skeptics — in the refusal to judge at all, but the final goal is the same for all of them — ataraxia, the imperturbability of the soul in the face of a world that the individual no longer controls.
[09:41–11:20] SECTION 4. NEOPLATONISM: THE ASCENT TO THE ONE

In the third century CE, Plotinus creates a system that will become the final and most influential synthesis of pagan ancient philosophy — Neoplatonism. Starting from the Platonic hierarchy of Forms headed by the Form of the Good, which we spoke about in the previous lecture, Plotinus builds an even more radical vertical hierarchy of reality headed by the One — a principle so simple and so superior to any possible definition that, strictly speaking, one cannot even say of it that it "exists," since the very concept of existence already introduces some limitation and multiplicity.

From the One, through a necessary but not conscious outpouring, emanation, arises Intellect, nous — the sphere of pure thought, where the Platonic Forms dwell; from Intellect emanates the World Soul, psyche, which in turn brings forth the material world as its lowest boundary, the one most removed from the One. Matter in Plotinus turns out to be almost identical with evil and non-being — not because it is demonically active, but because it represents the limit, the extreme point of removal from the perfection of the One, where the light of the intelligible Good is almost completely exhausted. The task of the human soul, cast into the material world, is the return path, an ascent through purification, catharsis, and contemplation back to Intellect and further to mystical union with the One itself, which is attained no longer by reasoning, but by a special supra-rational ecstasy. Neoplatonism will exert a colossal influence on Christian thought, above all through Augustine, to whom we now turn, since the very structure of the soul's ascent from the lower to the higher, from multiplicity to unity, fit perfectly with the Christian understanding of the soul's path to God.
[11:20–14:29] SECTION 5. PATRISTICS: AUGUSTINE AND PHILOSOPHY AS CONFESSION

From the fourth century CE, philosophy finds itself faced with a challenge unknown to classical antiquity — the need to make sense of belief in one personal, omnipotent God, who created the world out of nothing and enters into direct, loving relations with each individual soul. Patristics — the collective work of the Church Fathers, who tried to express the content of Christian revelation in the language of Greek philosophy — reaches its peak in the person of Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, who lived from 354 to 430.

Augustine, who in his youth was drawn to Manichaeism and to the Neoplatonism of Plotinus, whom we have just discussed, after an agonizing spiritual search described in his autobiographical Confessions, comes to Christianity and creates a philosophy that is fundamentally different in its very genre from everything we have analyzed earlier: the Confessions is written not as a treatise proving theses to an impartial reader, but as a prayerful address to God, in which the philosophical analysis of memory, time, and will is inseparably intertwined with personal repentance. It is precisely in the Confessions that Augustine formulates one of the deepest philosophical investigations into the nature of time in the history of thought: he notes that the past no longer exists, the future does not yet exist, and the present slips elusively away the moment we try to fix it — and he concludes that time exists not as an objective substance, but as the stretching of the soul itself, distentio animi, which holds within itself memory of the past, attention to the present, and expectation of the future.

Augustine's key philosophical innovation is the doctrine of the will as an independent capacity of the soul, not reducible either to reason or to desire: Greek philosophy, as we saw in the example of Socrates, held that a person who has known the good will automatically begin to strive for it — for the Greeks, vice was above all a consequence of ignorance. Augustine, starting from his own painful experience described in the famous episode of the stolen pears from his youth, insists: a human being can clearly see the good and consciously choose evil — this capacity of the will to deviate from the known good is true freedom, but at the same time also the source of sin, which, according to Augustine, is rooted in the original sin of Adam, because of which the will of all humanity becomes damaged and unable to turn to the good without the assistance of divine grace.

Especially important for our course is Augustine's late politico-philosophical work The City of God, written in response to the sack of Rome by the Goths in 410 CE and to the accusations of pagans that the cause of the catastrophe was the empire's rejection of the old gods. Augustine puts forward the concept of two cities intertwined in earthly history, but fundamentally different in their ultimate aim: the earthly city, civitas terrena, unites people driven by love of self to the point of contempt for God, while the City of God, civitas Dei, unites people driven by love of God to the point of contempt for self. No earthly state, including Rome itself, can be identified with the City of God, and none deserves an absolute loyalty of religious intensity — an important thesis limiting the claims of any political power to a sacred status, to which we will return when examining theories of political legitimacy in the relevant lectures of the course.
[14:29–17:08] SECTION 6. SCHOLASTICISM: THOMAS AQUINAS AND THE SYNTHESIS OF FAITH AND REASON

Eight centuries after Augustine, in the thirteenth century, scholasticism takes shape in the universities of Western Europe — a method of philosophizing built on the systematic application of Aristotelian logic to theological questions, a form of university disputation that proceeds by stating a thesis, considering the objections to it, and refuting them one by one. The culmination of scholasticism is the work of Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican friar who taught at the University of Paris, whose main work, the Summa Theologiae, is a grand attempt to systematize all Christian theology by means of the Aristotelian philosophy that had only just been rediscovered for the West, largely through Arab commentators such as Ibn Rushd, whom we mentioned in the first lecture.

Unlike Augustine, for whom reason acts primarily within faith and in the light of grace, Thomas, following Aristotle, grants natural reason a considerable sphere of competence of its own, accessible to human beings independently of revelation. Hence the famous five proofs of the existence of God, the five ways, each of which starts from some obvious fact of sense experience — the existence of motion, causal chains, contingent and necessary things, degrees of perfection, purposiveness in nature — and rises from it to the necessity of a first cause, which Thomas identifies with God. Note the direct connection between the fifth way, the argument from purposiveness, and the Aristotelian doctrine of the unmoved mover, which we analyzed in the previous lecture: Thomas in effect Christianizes Aristotelian metaphysics, identifying the philosophical unmoved mover, pure thought thinking itself, with the personal God of biblical revelation.

Thomas also constructs a complete hierarchy of laws, important for the material on social and political philosophy later in the course: eternal law, the rational divine plan for governing the universe; natural law, the reflection of eternal law in the rational nature of the human being, accessible to knowledge by natural reason without any revelation; and human, positive law, the concrete enactments of individual states, which acquire moral binding force only insofar as they do not contradict natural law. This concept will become one of the most important sources of the later theory of natural rights, to which we will turn in our discussion of the political philosophy of the early modern period.

The characteristic form of scholastic thinking itself is the quaestio disputata, the disputed question: the teacher formulates a thesis, listens to and records all possible objections to it, however numerous they may be, and then successively, point by point, answers each of them before confirming the original thesis in a more precise form. This method, which requires that the strongest version of the opposing position be presented honestly before it is refuted, clearly continues that same tradition of rational argument and openness to counterargument that we trace throughout the course starting with the Milesian school — proof that scholasticism, despite its reputation as a dogmatic discipline, was in essence a deeply polemical, dialogical undertaking.
[17:08–19:41] SECTION 7. THE DISPUTE OVER UNIVERSALS

For several centuries medieval philosophy is permeated by a dispute, going back to the disagreement between Plato and Aristotle, about the status of general concepts, universals — such as "human being in general," "whiteness in general," "justice in general." The question is formulated in the sharpest possible way: do genera and species exist in reality, independently of individual things and human thinking, or are they only names, words by which we designate similarity between individual things, while in reality only these individual things exist?

Extreme realism, going back to the Platonic understanding of Forms as independently existing entities, maintains that universals really exist, before things, as their eternal prototypes. Moderate realism, developed by Thomas Aquinas following Aristotle, takes an intermediate position: universals exist in things, as their form, but also in the human mind, as a concept abstracted from the perception of many similar individual things — that is, the universal is real, but does not exist separately from individual things and the thinking mind. Nominalism, most vividly represented in the fourteenth century by William of Ockham, takes the diametrically opposite extreme position: only individual things really exist, while universals are nothing more than names, nomina, convenient labels that the mind creates to group similar individual objects; general concepts have no independent reality of their own, either in things or before them.

Ockham formulated the famous methodological principle that entered history as Ockham's razor: one should not multiply entities beyond necessity — if individual things are enough to explain a phenomenon, there is no need to additionally postulate the existence of universals as separate realities. Between extreme realism and nominalism, Pierre Abelard in the twelfth century proposed his own solution, developing a position known as conceptualism: universals do not exist as separate things either before things or after them, but they are not empty words either — they are concepts that the mind actually forms on the basis of a real similarity between individual things, and therefore have a kind of intermediate status, real as a cognitive operation, but not as an independently existing entity. This dispute, which may seem like a purely abstract scholastic game, in fact had colossal consequences for the later history of philosophy and science: the nominalist attitude that only individual, empirically observable facts are real, while general concepts are only convenient tools of the mind, became one of the most important philosophical premises of the empiricism of the early modern period, which we will examine in detail in the fifth lecture of the course in connection with Bacon and Locke.
[19:41–20:54] CONCLUSION

Let us summarize the long journey from the death of Alexander the Great to the threshold of the early modern period. The three Hellenistic schools — Stoicism, Epicureanism, and Skepticism — despite the differences in their physical and metaphysical premises, converged on one practical goal: to attain peace of mind, ataraxia, in a world that had ceased to be commensurate with the individual human being. Plotinus's Neoplatonism built a mystical vertical of ascent from matter through Intellect to the One, preparing the conceptual apparatus for the encounter between Greek philosophy and Christian revelation. Augustine turned philosophy into confession, opening up the depth of the inner, volitional life of the person and the nature of time as the stretching out of the soul. Thomas Aquinas synthesized Aristotelian logic with Christian theology, building a hierarchy of eternal, natural, and human law. And the dispute between realists and nominalists over universals, which ended with Ockham's razor, prepared the ground for the empirical revolution of the early modern period.

In the next lecture we will see how the Renaissance humanists rediscover the dignity of the individual human being, and how the philosophers of the early modern period — Bacon, Descartes, Spinoza, Leibniz, Locke, and Hume — split into two great camps, empiricists and rationalists, in search of a new, much more rigorous method for attaining reliable knowledge, in place of both the scholastic and the purely contemplative ancient tradition.
MATERIALS FOR REINFORCEMENT
Key Concepts
Stoicism: logos, apatheia, indifferents, cosmopolis (Zeno, Epictetus, Marcus Aurelius)
Epicureanism: ataraxia, clinamen, atomism, the contract theory of justice
Skepticism: isostheneia, epoché, Pyrrhonism and Academic skepticism (Pyrrho, Carneades)
Neoplatonism: the One, emanation, Intellect (nous), World Soul (Plotinus)
Patristics: time as distentio animi, will and the Fall, the two cities (Augustine)
Scholasticism: the five ways, eternal/natural/human law, quaestio disputata (Thomas Aquinas)
The dispute over universals: realism, nominalism, conceptualism, Ockham's razor
Recommended Reading
Marcus Aurelius. Meditations.
Augustine. Confessions, Book XI (on time).
Augustine. The City of God, Book XIV.
Thomas Aquinas. Summa Theologiae, Part I, Question 2.
Self-Check Questions
What is the Stoic distinction between what depends on us and what does not depend on us, and how is it connected to the concept of apatheia?
How does the clinamen solve the problem of free will in Epicurus's atomistic physics?
Compare Pyrrhonian and Academic skepticism, taking the position of Carneades as an example.
How did the structure of emanation in Plotinus's Neoplatonism (the One — Intellect — World Soul) prepare the conceptual apparatus for Christian thought?
What is the difference between Socrates' position and Augustine's position on the nature of vice and free will?
Formulate the three positions in the dispute over universals (realism, nominalism, conceptualism) and name their representatives.

items.title: 14. Social Philosophy
lines: Lecture 14. Social Philosophy
Society as a system; philosophy of history; concepts of social progress; civil society and the state; the problem of freedom and justice
[00:00–02:33] Introduction

When we speak of "society," we usually do not stop to think about what lies behind this word: is it merely the sum of separate individuals living side by side, or is it something greater — a whole that possesses its own laws of existence, which cannot be reduced to the psychology of any single person? It is precisely this question — what society is and how it is organized — that opens the field of philosophical knowledge called social philosophy. Unlike sociology, which empirically studies specific social structures and processes, social philosophy asks more fundamental questions: does society exist as an independent reality, or is it merely a convenient abstraction for describing the interactions of individuals; does the history of humankind have a direction and meaning, or is it a chaotic sequence of chance events; what are we entitled to call social progress, and does it exist at all; how are civil society and the state related; and, finally, what genuine freedom and justice are, and whether they are compatible with one another in principle.

Today's lecture will examine these five themes in sequence. We will begin with the question of society as a system — with the classic dispute between social holism and social individualism. Then we will turn to the philosophy of history, analyzing linear and cyclical models of the historical process. Next we will consider concepts of social progress and the famous critique of historicism. After that we will move on to the distinction between civil society and the state, beginning with theories of the social contract. We will conclude the lecture with an analysis of the problem of freedom and justice — the central theme of modern and contemporary political philosophy. Each of these themes bears directly on everyday life: when we argue about whether the state should regulate the economy, intervene in the private lives of citizens, or reduce inequality, we are, often without realizing it, relying on certain philosophical assumptions about the nature of society, the direction of history, and the relation of freedom to justice — and the ability to identify these assumptions makes our political judgments much better grounded.

It should also be added that all five themes of today's lecture are not isolated academic puzzles, but the very hidden axioms on which real political programs are built: the dispute between liberals and socialists, the dispute between supporters of traditional institutions and radical reformers, the dispute over the permissible limits of state intervention in the economy — all of these are ultimately disputes about the philosophy of history, the nature of society, and the relation between freedom and justice, even if the participants in these disputes rarely formulate their disagreements in such terms.
[02:33–06:33] 1. Society as a System

The first fundamental question of social philosophy is the question of the ontological status of society: does society exist as a reality irreducible to the individuals that compose it, or is society merely a convenient label for the totality of interacting people? The position affirming the first is commonly called social holism (from Greek ὅλος, "whole"): according to this view, society is a system possessing emergent properties — that is, properties that cannot be explained by studying individual persons separately, just as the properties of water cannot be derived from studying a single atom of hydrogen or oxygen. A classical representative of holism is the French sociologist and philosopher Émile Durkheim, who introduced the concept of the "social fact" — ways of acting, thinking, and feeling that exist outside the individual and exert coercive force upon them; the language we speak, the legal norms to which we submit, the religious ideas inherited from our ancestors — all of this, for Durkheim, existed before the birth of every particular person and will exist after their death, and therefore constitutes a reality of a special, supra-individual order.

The opposite position is social (methodological) individualism, according to which any explanation of social phenomena must ultimately be reduced to the actions, intentions, and beliefs of individual persons; society, from this point of view, has no will or consciousness of its own, and talk about how "society wants" or "society demands" is nothing more than a convenient metaphor concealing a set of individual decisions. The Austrian economist and philosopher Friedrich Hayek and his teacher Ludwig von Mises insisted precisely on this position, warning about the danger of what they called "collectivist fictions" — the idea of society, class, or nation as a single acting subject capable of having its own goals, which, in their view, opens the way to totalitarian political projects that sacrifice the individual to an abstract "whole."

An intermediate position is taken by so-called moderate methodological holism, which recognizes that social structures exert a real causal influence on individuals — shaping their beliefs, opportunities, and even their very self-understanding — but insists at the same time that these structures themselves are reproduced and changed exclusively through the actions and interactions of living people, and therefore do not exist as something completely independent of individual activity; this position, developed in particular by the British sociologist Anthony Giddens in his "theory of structuration," seeks to overcome the rigid dichotomy of holism and individualism by showing that structure and agency stand in a relation of mutual, rather than one-sided, conditioning.

A third, more balanced approach was proposed by the American sociologist Talcott Parsons within the framework of structural functionalism: society is understood as a system of interconnected subsystems — economic, political, legal, and cultural — each of which performs a definite function necessary for preserving the integrity and stability of the system as a whole, just as the organs of a biological organism perform specialized functions that ensure the organism's survival. Critics of functionalism, among them the German philosopher and sociologist Ralf Dahrendorf, pointed out that this model places excessive emphasis on equilibrium and stability, overlooking the role of conflict, of the struggle for resources and power, as the driving force of social change — which brings us directly to the next topic, the philosophy of history, where the question of the character of historical dynamics comes to the fore.

It is also worth mentioning the position of the German sociologist Max Weber, who proposed a kind of compromise between holism and individualism through the method of "interpretive sociology" (verstehende Soziologie): according to Weber, social phenomena must be explained through the reconstruction of the subjective meaning that individuals themselves attach to their actions, but at the same time the result of many individual actions is regularly the emergence of supra-individual structures — such as Weber's concept of the "iron cage" of rationalization, an impersonal bureaucratic system which, once it arises from the totality of rational individual decisions, begins to dominate the individuals themselves and limit their freedom in a way that none of them individually intended.
[06:33–10:51] 2. The Philosophy of History

The philosophy of history asks whether the historical process has an inner logic, direction, and meaning, or whether history is merely a sequence of unrelated events. One of the first philosophical models of history was proposed by the Italian thinker Giambattista Vico at the beginning of the eighteenth century. He developed a cyclical theory according to which all peoples pass through the same stages — the "Age of Gods," the "Age of Heroes," and the "Age of Men" — after which the cycle repeats in the form of the so-called "return," ricorso. The cyclical model of history was also characteristic of ancient thought as a whole: the Greeks and Romans were inclined to see history as a cycle of the birth, flourishing, and decline of civilizations rather than as a progressive movement toward some goal.

A fundamentally different, linear and teleological model of history was proposed by the Christian worldview, and then in secularized form by German classical philosophy, above all Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. For Hegel, world history is a process of the gradual self-disclosure of absolute spirit through dialectical development — the famous triad of thesis, antithesis, and synthesis — and each historical epoch makes its necessary contribution to this movement toward the final goal, which Hegel defined as spirit becoming aware of its own freedom. History, for Hegel, is a "progress in the consciousness of freedom," and world events, however tragic they may seem to individual participants, contribute to this movement — an idea expressed in his famous image of the "cunning of reason" (List der Vernunft), according to which the individual passions and ambitions of historical actors unconsciously serve the realization of a broader rational design.

Karl Marx, strongly influenced by Hegel but inverting his idealism in a materialist key, proposed his own teleological scheme: history is driven not by ideas and not by the world spirit, but by the material productive forces and relations of production, and the succession of socio-economic formations — from the primitive communal system through slavery, feudalism, and capitalism to communism — is a lawful, objective process conditioned by the internal contradictions of each formation. A substantially different position was taken by thinkers who denied the very existence of a single historical process: the German philosopher Oswald Spengler and the British historian Arnold Toynbee proposed cyclical models according to which not humanity as a whole, but separate local civilizations, follow their own path of birth, flourishing, and inevitable decline, like living organisms — which renders meaningless any talk of a single, universal progress of humanity as such.

Also worth mentioning is the earlier conception of the Arab historian and philosopher Ibn Khaldun, which in many ways anticipated these ideas: in the fourteenth century he proposed a theory of the cyclical succession of dynasties. According to Ibn Khaldun, the driving force of historical dynamics is "asabiyya" — group solidarity and cohesion, which allows young communities, not yet softened by luxury, to seize power from aging ruling dynasties, only then, as wealth accumulates and morals decline, to travel the same road of moral decay themselves and in turn give way to new, more cohesive contenders for power — a cycle that, in Ibn Khaldun's view, repeats regardless of the specific cultural context.

It is also important to emphasize that the difference between linear and cyclical models of history is not merely a matter of theoretical curiosity, but a matter that has direct practical consequences: if history really moves toward a definite goal, then political action is justified in accelerating this movement, sometimes at the cost of significant sacrifices; if history is cyclical or lacks direction altogether, then the far more reasonable strategy is not to race ahead in revolutionary fashion but to carefully maintain institutional stability and gradually correct specific shortcomings.
[10:51–13:53] 3. Concepts of Social Progress

The idea of social progress — the notion that human history moves toward better living conditions, wider knowledge, and growing morality and justice — flourished in the Enlightenment. The French philosopher and mathematician Nicolas de Condorcet, who wrote his famous Sketch for a Historical Picture of the Progress of the Human Mind in prison, on the eve of his execution, was convinced that the development of science, the spread of education, and the improvement of political institutions inevitably lead humankind to a state of ever greater well-being, equality, and freedom from prejudice. Optimistic faith in progress permeated a significant part of European philosophical and political thought in the nineteenth century, finding expression both in liberal theories of social development and in the Marxist concept of the inevitable transition to a classless society.

However, the twentieth century, with its two world wars, totalitarian regimes, and the practice of mass extermination of people, subjected the idea of linear progress to radical doubt. The Austrian-British philosopher Karl Popper, in his work The Poverty of Historicism, criticized the very methodological stance that he called historicism — the belief that history is governed by objective laws that make it possible to predict its future course scientifically. Popper argued that such predictions are logically untenable, since the course of history depends crucially on the growth of human knowledge, and the growth of knowledge is fundamentally unpredictable: if we could predict the content of a future scientific discovery, we would already have made that discovery today.

Moreover, Popper pointed to the dangerous political cost of historicist thinking: the conviction that one knows the laws of history easily turns into a justification of violence in the name of an "inevitable" future, and those who disagree with the official version of historical regularity are declared enemies of progress, to be eliminated — that is precisely how, in Popper's view, historicist ideas legitimized the practice of the totalitarian regimes of the twentieth century. In place of historicism, Popper proposed the concept of an "open society" — a society that renounces the claim to know history's final goal and instead is built on the principles of gradual, testable, and reversible social reform, critical rationalism, and tolerance of diverse opinions.

Contemporary discussions of progress try to avoid both the naive optimism of the Enlightenment and complete relativism: most philosophers today agree that one can speak of progress in individual, limited areas — for example, in the spread of medical knowledge, the reduction of violent deaths, or the expansion of human rights — without claiming at the same time that history as a whole is moving toward any predetermined final goal. A striking example of the danger of premature claims about the end of historical development is the much-discussed thesis of the American political scientist Francis Fukuyama about the "end of history," put forward after the end of the Cold War: Fukuyama argued that liberal democracy and the market economy represent the final form of human social organization, one without any reasonable alternative, and that all countries of the world will sooner or later arrive at it — a thesis that came under severe criticism as the following decades demonstrated the resilience of authoritarian alternatives and new forms of political instability, once again confirming Popper's caution with respect to any claims to knowledge of the final point of historical movement.
[13:53–16:53] 4. Civil Society and the State

The distinction between civil society and the state is one of the central themes of modern political philosophy, rooted in the theories of the social contract of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The English philosopher Thomas Hobbes, in his treatise Leviathan, described the pre-state "state of nature" as a "war of all against all," in which human life, in his famous formulation, is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short"; to avoid this state of mutual destruction, people enter into a social contract, voluntarily giving up part of their natural freedom in favor of the sovereign — the state — which in return ensures security and order. John Locke, unlike Hobbes, believed the state of nature to be not so catastrophic, but unstable because of the absence of an independent arbiter in disputes over property and justice; for Locke, the state is created first and foremost to protect natural human rights — to life, liberty, and property — and if the government systematically violates these rights, the people retain the right to rebellion.

It was precisely the Lockean tradition that formed the basis of the liberal concept of the limited state and the separation of powers. Civil society in the modern philosophical sense is the sphere of voluntary associations independent of state control: professional associations, religious communities, charitable organizations, independent mass media — a sphere that lies between the private life of the individual and the formal institutions of state power. Hegel, and after him Alexis de Tocqueville, attached special importance to civil society as a space in which individuals learn cooperation, compromise, and collective action without waiting for instructions from above; Tocqueville, in his famous work on American democracy, noted that it is precisely the numerous voluntary associations of citizens that serve as the main protection against the danger both of minority despotism and of the "tyranny of the majority," which he considered one of the main threats to democratic society.

The Italian Marxist theorist Antonio Gramsci proposed a more critical understanding of civil society as a space in which the ruling class establishes its cultural and ideological dominance — hegemony — securing the consent of the governed not so much through coercion as through shaping the idea that the existing order of things is natural and inevitable. The relationship between a strong civil society and a moderate, limited state is today regarded by many philosophers as the most important condition for a stable democracy: where civil society is weak or suppressed, the state tends to degenerate either into an authoritarian or into a paternalistic system, deprived of mechanisms of independent public control.

It is also worth recalling the position of Jean-Jacques Rousseau, whose concept of the "general will" (volonté générale) occupies a special, in many respects ambiguous place in this tradition: for Rousseau, true freedom consists not in the absence of any subordination, but in obedience to a law that citizens establish for themselves as participants in a political community — an idea that inspired the democratic tradition of popular sovereignty, but at the same time, according to Rousseau's critics, contains the danger of justifying coercion of the minority in the name of a "general will" supposedly expressed by the majority, which brings this concept close to the problem of positive freedom that we will consider in the next section.
[16:53–19:54] 5. The Problem of Freedom and Justice

The concluding theme of today's lecture is the relationship between freedom and justice, two concepts that in political philosophy often enter into a tense relationship with each other. The British philosopher Isaiah Berlin, in his famous lecture "Two Concepts of Liberty," distinguished between negative freedom — freedom "from" external interference, that is, the absence of coercion by other people or the state — and positive freedom — freedom "for" self-realization, that is, the ability to be master of one's own life and to make use of one's own capacities. Berlin warned that the concept of positive freedom was historically often used to justify authoritarian intervention in people's lives under the slogan of liberating their "true" or "higher" "self" from their own supposedly irrational desires — a mechanism that lay at the basis of many totalitarian ideologies of the twentieth century.

The American philosopher John Rawls, in his foundational work A Theory of Justice, proposed an influential concept of justice as fairness, based on the thought experiment of the "veil of ignorance": let us imagine that the participants in the social contract choose the principles for organizing society without knowing in advance what position in that society they themselves will occupy — whether they will be rich or poor, gifted or not, members of the majority or of a minority. Rawls argued that under such conditions rational people would choose two principles: first, the broadest possible and equal system of basic liberties for all; second, the so-called difference principle, which allows social and economic inequality only to the extent that it brings the greatest benefit to the least advantaged members of society.

Rawls's theory provoked a strong response and criticism from both sides of the political spectrum: the American libertarian philosopher Robert Nozick, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia, argued that compulsory redistribution of property in the name of greater equality violates the rights of individuals to what they have honestly earned, comparing state redistribution to a form of forced labor; communitarian critics, including Michael Sandel and Alasdair MacIntyre, pointed out that the abstract "participant" in Rawls's veil of ignorance is a fiction, since real people are always embedded in concrete communities, traditions, and relationships that cannot be bracketed out when discussing justice. The dispute between supporters of the libertarian, liberal egalitarian, and communitarian traditions remains unresolved to this day, reflecting a deeper contradiction between the value of individual freedom of choice and the value of collective responsibility for the well-being of all members of society.

The Indian economist and philosopher Amartya Sen proposed an alternative approach that in many respects reconciles both sides of the dispute, known as the "capability approach": instead of measuring a person's well-being through income or the resources at their disposal, Sen proposed assessing their real capabilities — what a person is able to do and what they are able to be — since the same income may mean a completely different degree of actual freedom depending on health, education, social status, or the discrimination a person faces, and therefore a just society is obliged to care not only about formal equality of rights, but also about real equality of opportunity to use them.
[19:54–21:51] Conclusion

In summary, let us note that all five themes discussed today are linked by a single logic: how we understand the nature of society — as an organic whole or as a collection of individuals — determines how we understand the driving forces of history; whether we believe in objective laws of historical progress or reject historicism in favor of an open, gradually reformable society determines our attitude toward state intervention in citizens' lives; and how we draw the line between civil society and the state is directly tied to the question of balance between negative freedom as noninterference and positive justice as redistribution. A useful image to remember is a pair of scales with two pans: on one pan lies the individual's freedom to dispose of their life and property without outside interference, on the other lies justice as society's care for its least protected members, and the pointer of these scales has throughout the history of political philosophy swung now one way, now the other, never settling permanently at either pole.

In the next lecture we will turn to the philosophy of culture and the philosophy of religion, where we will see how the categories of society, history, and justice discussed today relate to broader questions about the meaning of human existence, cultural identity, and the place of the sacred in social life — that is, we will see how social philosophy is connected to more fundamental layers of philosophical knowledge about the human being. An image of a single chain of questions will help you remember today's material: our idea of society as a whole or as a sum of individuals shapes our idea of the driving forces of history; our view of whether objective laws of history exist shapes our attitude toward the idea of progress and the permissible limits of social reform; and our view of the balance between civil society and the state directly determines how we answer the final question of the lecture — the question of the fragile equilibrium between individual freedom and justice toward society as a whole.

source.title: 4. Эллинистическая и римская философия. Средневековая философия

lines: 4-дәріс. Эллинистік және Рим философиясы. Ортағасырлық философия
Стоицизм, эпикуреизм, скептицизм, неоплатонизм; патристика (Августин); схоластика (Фома Аквинский); универсалиялар туралы дау.

Біздің дәуірімізге дейінгі 323 жылы Александр Македонский қайтыс болады, ал оның өлімімен бірге тек империя ғана емес, бүкіл грек өмірінің қалыптасқан көкжиегі де күйрейді. Сократ жолында өлімге барған, ал Платон мен Аристотель саяси утопияларын соған арнап құрған полис — өзіне-өзі жеткілікті қала-мемлекет — енді жеке адам үшін әлемнің орталығы болудан қалады: енді ол алып, тұлғасыз эллинистік монархияларда өмір сүреді, онда шешімдер одан алыста қабылданады және оның еркіне тәуелді ештеңе дерлік қалмайды. Кеше ғана космостың құрылымы мен идеал мемлекеттің табиғаты туралы ұлы сұрақтармен айналысқан философия енді әлдеқайда өзекті әрі жеке сұраққа жауап беруге мәжбүр болады: жеке адам енді өзі билемейтін әлемде ішкі тыныштығы мен қадір-қасиетін қалай сақтай алады?

Бүгін біз ұзақ жолдан өтеміз — практикалық даналықтың эллинистік мектептерінен, стоицизмнен, эпикурейшілдіктен және скептицизмнен бастап, неоплатонизмнің мистикалық синтезі арқылы, грек философиясы христиандықпен кездесіп, жеке тұлғалы, құдіреті шексіз Құдай идеясы тұрғысынан өзінің барлық ұғымдарын қайта ойлауға мәжбүр болатын сәтке дейін барамыз. Біз Августинді көреміз, ол үшін философия тәубеге айналады, және Фома Аквинскийді көреміз, ол сегіз ғасырдан кейін сенім мен ақылды аристотельдік логика құралдарымен бітістіруге тырысады, ал соңында тарихтағы ең ұзақ әрі өнімді философиялық даулардың бірімен — универсалиялар туралы даумен — аяқтаймыз; бұл дау бірнеше ғасыр бойы еуропалық ойдың жалпы ұғымдар мен дара заттардың арақатынасын қалай түсінетінін айқындайды.
[01:27–04:08] БӨЛІМ 1. СТОИЦИЗМ: ТАБИҒАТПЕН КЕЛІСІМ АРҚЫЛЫ ЕРКІНДІК

Стоиктер мектебін Афинада біздің дәуірімізге дейінгі шамамен 300 жылы Китиондық Зенон негіздеді; мектеп өз атауын ол әңгімелер жүргізген портиктен — Суретті Стоядан алды. Стоиктік физиканың негізінде космос — логос сіңген, парасатпен реттелген, жанды біртұтас бүтін деген түсінік жатыр; логос ұғымы, бірінші дәрістен есіңізде болар, Гераклиттен бастау алады. Әлемде болып жатқанның бәрі себептердің қатаң тізбегіне, тағдырға, жазмышқа бағынады, және жекелеген бірде-бір оқиға ол болып жатқаннан өзге түрде бола алмайды.

Осы физикадан стоиктер мектептің ең ықпалды мұрасына айналған этиканы шығарады. Егер әлемдегі барлық нәрсені парасатты құдайлық қамқорлық алдын ала айқындаса, онда шын мәнінде біздің билігімізде бар жалғыз нәрсе — сыртқы жағдайлар емес, соларға қатысты өз пайымымыз, болып жатқанға келісуіміз немесе келіспеуіміз. Келесі дәрісте біз Қайта Өрлеу дәуірінің гуманистері жеке адамның қадір-қасиетін қалай қайта ашатынын, ал Жаңа заман философтары — Бэкон, Декарт, Спиноза, Лейбниц, Локк және Юм — схоластикалық дәстүрді де, таза ой-толғамдық антикалық дәстүрді де алмастыратын, сенімді білімге жетудің жаңа, әлдеқайда қатаң әдісін іздеп, эмпириктер мен рационалистер деген екі үлкен лагерьге қалай бөлінетінін көреміз.

Өзін-өзі тексеру сұрақтары
Бізге тәуелді нәрсе мен бізге тәуелді емес нәрсені стоиктік ажырату неде және ол апатия ұғымымен қалай байланысты?
Клинамен Эпикурдың атомистік физикасындағы ерік бостандығы мәселесін қалай шешеді?
Карнеадтың ұстанымы мысалында пиррондық және академиялық скептицизмді салыстырыңыз.
Плотиннің неоплатонизміндегі эманация құрылымы (Біртұтас — Ақыл — Әлемдік жан) христиандық ой үшін ұғымдық аппаратты қалай әзірледі?
Азғындықтың табиғаты мен ерік бостандығы мәселесінде Сократтың ұстанымы мен Августиннің ұстанымы арасындағы айырмашылық неде?
Универсалиялар туралы даудағы үш ұстанымды (реализм, номинализм, концептуализм) тұжырымдап, олардың өкілдерін атаңыз.
